answer.rationale:
The forcing constraints narrow the field: the primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew, so a no-action path (defer_decision) creates a supply gap on a line already at 94% of committed volume. negotiate_terms is largely foreclosed because the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, so memory_c4's benchmarking lever has no surface to act on. renew_incumbent (memory_c1, memory_c6) preserves delivery stability but cannot deliver the mandated 18% cut, since volume pricing requires a multi-year commitment the incumbent will not reprice now. That leaves the low-cost vendor, whose quote meets the mandate alone.

But memory_c2 is the single load-bearing claim behind that move, and it is the one I trust least on its face: it is dated ('last year'), it summarizes cost and invoicing accuracy but is silent on on-time delivery, ramp rate, and sustained volume at committed levels, and it does not state whether the win was on this component class or a different one. A summary that survived consolidation because it read as a clean success is exactly the kind that can shed its qualifiers. So I am pulling the source record for memory_c2 to check scope, volume, and whether any delivery misses were dropped in consolidation. I am also pulling memory_c3, because the second-source record is the only inherited evidence about how this supply base behaves under allocation stress, and it may show that the constrained-component fix was vendor-specific rather than a general capability.

Intended action is a switch of primary supply, but explicitly at guarded scale: qualify and cut over a bounded share of volume first with the incumbent's tail or spot coverage held for the remainder, rather than a clean full-line cutover. At 94% utilization with zero buffer, a cost win that arrives with a two-week ramp stumble is a net loss on the stated objective, which bars increasing delivery risk, not just minimizing cost. If verification shows memory_c2's win came at lower volume or on a different component, I will fall back to a short bridge with the incumbent and carry the switch into the next review rather than absorb the risk blind.

Downstream risk: the mandate is a cost target, and optimizing to it can quietly convert delivery reliability into a tradeable variable. The 18% number should not be allowed to overwrite the no-added-delivery-risk constraint that sits beside it.
